title: Metal scrap value chains and global benchmarking for green manufacturing and industrial decarbonization
abstract: Abstract Industrial decarbonization is increasingly constrained by technology choice, availability and quality of resources. Metal scrap can lower emissions in metal production as it can substitute for primary iron and other metal routes with substantially lower energy demand, especially when paired with low-carbon electricity. Yet the climate benefit of scrap-based production is dependent on reliable end-of-life capture, effective sorting and pre-processing, impurity control during melting and refining, and governance arrangements that treat scrap as a strategic industrial input rather than residual waste. While these challenges apply across metal recycling systems, this study focuses primarily on the iron and steel sector, which represents the largest and most structurally developed global scrap market. This study conducts a targeted literature review combined with international benchmarking to examine the metal scrap value chain and its role in supporting green manufacturing and industrial decarbonization. Scrap system performance and policy configurations are compared across five major steel economies to identify transferable lessons. The analysis shows that scrap availability alone does not guarantee high utilization; rather, furnace structure, electricity conditions, market organization, and quality standards jointly determine scrap absorption. Advanced systems achieve higher effective recycling through formalized collection, extended producer responsibility, standardized grading, and investment in sensor-based sorting and dismantling practices, while fragmented and informal-heavy systems face persistent losses and quality variability. Although the benchmarking focuses on iron and steel systems, the findings highlight systemic challenges—such as collection efficiency, material purity management, and governance coordination—that are broadly relevant to other metal recycling systems, including non-ferrous metals.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Climate change is one of the most urgent challenges of the twenty-first century, with profound implications for ecosystems, economies, and human well-being. Global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reached ~ 57.4 gigatonnes CO 2 -eq in 2022 [ 1 ] and current policies place the world on track for ~ 2.7 °C warming by 2100 [ 2 ]. The Paris Agreement, adopted in December 2015 and ratified by 194 countries as of 2023, reflects a near-universal recognition of the need for rapid decarbonization. Limiting global warming to below 2 °C, and ideally 1.5 °C, demands transformative action across all major emitting sectors.

The industrial sector is a significant contributor to global CO 2  emissions, responsible for approximately 30% of the total emissions [ 3 ,  4 ]. This includes emissions from energy-intensive industries such as cement, iron and steel production, oil refineries, and chemical production [ 5 ,  6 ]. The industrial sector, particularly manufacturing, contributes significantly to global GDP. The manufacturing sector alone accounts for approximately 15.7% of global GDP and contributes to 16.9% of global employment [ 7 ]. In specific countries, this contribution can be higher; for instance, Indonesia's manufacturing sector contributed 22% to its national GDP in 2012 and is projected to reach 30% by 2035 [ 8 ]. This dual role—as both an engine of economic growth and a major emitter—underscores the urgency of industrial decarbonization. Pathways to reduce emissions include the adoption of low-carbon technologies, improvements in energy and material efficiency, and the integration of circular economy approaches that promote the recovery and valorization of waste streams and secondary resources [ 9 ,  10 ]. Green manufacturing, in particular, has emerged as a critical strategy for minimizing environmental impacts through efficient resource use, reduced emissions, and waste minimization [ 11 ,  12 ]. It incorporates sustainable energy sources like solar and wind power, which can significantly reduce dependence on non-renewable fuels and mitigating greenhouse gas emissions [ 13 ,  14 ]. Furthermore, green manufacturing drives innovation by creating new environmentally friendly products and optimizing production processes [ 15 ]. Firms that invest in green innovations benefit from improved organizational capabilities and market advantages, which can lead to lower emissions and better environmental performance [ 16 ,  17 ].

Among industrial subsectors, the metal industry—especially the iron and steel sector— is a significant contributor to global CO 2  emissions. In 2020, the steel industry produced approximately 2.6 billion tonnes of CO 2 , accounting for 7–9% of global anthropogenic CO 2  emissions [ 18 ]. Iron and steel alone represent around 8% of energy-related emissions, with an average of 1.85 tonnes of CO 2  emitted for every tonne of steel produced [ 18 ,  19 ]. The challenge is particularly acute in primary steelmaking. The blast furnace–basic oxygen furnace (BF–BOF) route emits about 1700 kg CO 2  per tonne of hot metal, compared to 780 kg CO 2  per tonne via conventional direct reduced iron–electric arc furnace (DRI–EAF) routes [ 20 ,  21 ].

Decarbonizing the metal sector has become a global priority. A range of strategies have emerged, including deployment of breakthrough technologies (e.g., hydrogen-based direct reduction of iron, inert anodes in aluminium smelting), integration of renewable electricity, material efficiency improvements, and expansion of circular economy practices [ 22 ]. Among these, the utilization of metal scrap stands out as one of the most immediate and cost-effective levers for reducing emissions. Multiple projections anticipate the share of scrap input in steelmaking could rise to 45% or more by 2050, depending on industrial maturity, recycling technology, scrap availability, and supportive policy frameworks [ 23 ]. The climate benefits are substantial: scrap-electric arc furnace (scrap-EAF) steelmaking can reduce emissions by up to 75% compared to traditional BF–BOF methods. Recycling also delivers significant energy savings—up to 60–74% for steel and up to 95% for aluminium compared to primary production [ 24 ]. Despite these advantages, substantial technical and systemic barriers remain. The persistence of fossil fuels in high-temperature processes, limited availability and quality of scrap feedstock, technological challenges in separation and refining, and the capital-intensive nature of retrofitting facilities all slow progress. In addition, uneven global scrap availability, quality concerns, and trade restrictions complicate the scaling of scrap-based solutions [ 25 ,  26 – 27 ].

In Indonesia, the dynamics are both promising and concerning. With a population exceeding 270 million and a rapidly expanding manufacturing and infrastructure sector, Indonesia represents a large emerging industrial economy where material demand is increasing while recycling systems are still developing. Indonesia is the largest economy in Southeast Asia, accounting for roughly one-third of the region’s total gross domestic product (GDP) and significantly exceeding the economic size of other ASEAN members such as Thailand, Malaysia, and Vietnam [ 28 ]. Rapid urbanization, infrastructure expansion, and industrialization are fueling rising demand for metals. Steel consumption reached 17.4 million tons in 2023 and is projected to grow substantially in the coming decades [ 29 ]. Indonesia is also expected to remain the largest steel market in Southeast Asia as construction, transport infrastructure, and manufacturing sectors expand. Yet domestic production remains dominated by BF–BOF methods, with limited adoption of lower-carbon EAF technology. Furthermore, reliance on coal-based smelters in the iron, aluminium, and copper sectors has led to mounting environmental concerns [ 30 ,  31 ]. In these non-ferrous sectors, scrap recycling can play an important role in reducing energy consumption and emissions, as secondary aluminum and copper production typically requires significantly less energy than primary smelting from ores. The mining and quarrying sectors contributed approximately 4.6 million metric tons of CO 2  equivalent in 2020 [ 32 ], emphasizing the environmental cost of extractive industries. Compared with other major economies where structured policy support has enabled higher scrap utilization—such as the European Union (EU), China, and Japan—Indonesia’s scrap market underdeveloped [ 23 ]. At the same time, Indonesia has pledged to achieve net-zero emissions by 2060 or sooner, making industrial decarbonization a key component of its climate strategy. The gap between growing material demand and sustainability commitments underscores the need for transformative approaches. Positioning metal scrap as a central resource in the industrial value chain could significantly reduce emissions, conserve resources, and align Indonesia with global circular economy trends.

These conditions highlight a critical gap in Indonesia’s industrial decarbonization pathway: the sustainability of the scrap value chain. Strengthening this value chain is vital to reducing reliance on carbon-intensive primary production and to supporting the growth of a circular economy in the metals sector. While previous studies have examined aspects of metal recycling, scrap flows, and circular economy strategies in the steel industry, these analyses are often limited to specific technologies, regional markets, or individual stages of the recycling process [ 33 ,  34 – 35 ]. Comprehensive assessments of the scrap value chain that integrate technical, market, and policy dimensions, particularly in relation to industrial decarbonization, remain limited.

Addressing this issue requires, first, a comprehensive identification of the scrap value chain to understand the key factors influencing the sustainability of scrap provision for decarbonization and second, international benchmarking of global scrap industry practices to identify strategies and solutions that can inform Indonesia’s transition. This review responds to that gap by examining global lessons on scrap management and identifying pathways to enhance Indonesia’s scrap industry as part of a broader strategy for green manufacturing and industrial decarbonization. Beyond synthesizing existing literature, this study contributes theoretically by integrating perspectives from green manufacturing, circular economy, and industrial decarbonization within a unified metal scrap value chain framework. The paper conceptualizes scrap management not merely as a waste recovery activity but as a systemic industrial process linking product design, collection systems, material separation, and metallurgical refining. By combining value-chain analysis with international benchmarking, the study provides a structured perspective on how technological capabilities, institutional arrangements, and material flows jointly shape the effectiveness of scrap-based circular production systems.

sections.heading: Green manufacturing concept for sustainable industrial production
paragraphs: Green manufacturing provides the conceptual foundation for this review, as it embeds environmental sustainability into industrial production through reduced emissions, minimized waste, and efficient use of resources. By aligning industrial activity with climate mitigation goals, green manufacturing supports both environmental and economic resilience. It enhances operational efficiency, reduces regulatory and material costs, and strengthens competitiveness by integrating sustainability into process design, material selection, and supply chains [ 36 ,  37 ].

Building on these principles, scrap utilization becomes a critical strategy: it directly reduces reliance on virgin resources, supports closed-loop systems, and contributes to circular economy objectives. Core elements of green manufacturing—systems-based evaluation, resource optimization, and long-term ecological considerations—provide the basis for positioning scrap as a central lever in sustainable industrial production [ 38 ].

Closed-loop systems are central to this approach, as they capture residual value by integrating recycling, reuse, and remanufacturing into industrial operations. Such systems not only reduce landfill waste and virgin material demand but also offer economic benefits: investment costs can be reduced by 30–80% through reuse of production components and increased resource efficiency [ 39 ,  40 ]. Recycling within green manufacturing extends beyond basic recovery to advanced practices such as remanufacturing, product life extension, and material substitution [ 41 ]. Moreover, integrating cleaner technologies and renewable energy sources—such as energy-efficient machinery, automation, solar, and wind—can further reduces emissions and energy intensity.

Operationally, green manufacturing also relies on optimized logistics and digital technologies. Local sourcing, collaborative distribution networks, and real-time monitoring of resource use via IoT and AI all reduce transportation and production-related emissions. Collectively, these measures link green manufacturing to circular economy principles, positioning scrap utilization as a critical bridge between environmental sustainability and industrial productivity. This relationship is illustrated in Fig.  1 , where scrap utilization serves as the nexus between green manufacturing and circular economy systems. Similar system-level perspectives are presented in the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) International Resource Panel report on global metal recycling rates, which establishes standardized indicators—such as end-of-life recycling rate and recycling input rate—to assess metal recycling performance across the life cycle [ 42 ]. sections.heading: Metal scrap outlook
paragraphs: The global scrap market has grown substantially over the past two decades, driven by rising demand for recycled materials and stronger emphasis on sustainability. Between 2003 and 2016, the international scrap trade expanded by 30%, with metals comprising around 85% of all traded waste among G20 countries [ 43 ]. As of 2023, the global scrap recycling market was valued at US$407 billion and is projected to reach nearly US$569 billion by 2032, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 3.8% [ 44 ]. The Asia Pacific dominates the market, accounting for 51.29% of the global share in 2023 [ 44 ].

Globally, approximately 900 Mt of scrap are processed annually, meeting 40% of raw material needs for industrial production [ 45 ]. Ferrous metals, particularly steel, represent the largest share: in 2017, more than 600 Mt of steel scrap were recycled, with Europe sourcing over 56% of its steel production from scrap [ 46 ,  47 ]. Recycling steel reduces energy use by 60% and CO 2  emissions by 58% [ 48 ]. Non-ferrous metals such as aluminium and copper provide even greater energy savings. Recycling aluminium reduces energy demand by ~ 95% and cuts emissions by over 16 tons of CO 2  per ton of recycled material [ 49 ,  50 ]. Copper scrap utilization reduces CO 2  emissions by ~ 65% and saves up to 85% of the energy compared with primary mining and refining [ 46 ,  51 ]. The International Energy Agency projects that recycled copper could meet up to 40% of global demand by 2050, while aluminium scrap could supply 50% of demand if supported by improved collection and separation systems [ 52 ].

The economic footprint of scrap is equally significant. Around 110 Mt of scrap are traded annually [ 53 ]. In the US alone, the recycling industry generated US$117 billion in 2021, supported nearly 160,000 direct jobs, and contributed US$12.3 billion in tax revenues [ 54 ]. Scrap also plays an important role in the informal economy: in 2018, scrap metals represented 60% of traded solid waste by weight, highlighting their centrality to global resource recovery [ 43 ,  55 ].

From a resource classification perspective, scrap can be divided into ferrous and non-ferrous metals, and by origin into home scrap, fabrication scrap, and end-of-life (EoL) scrap [ 56 ]. Home scrap, also known as forming scrap, is generated during the primary production of metals within facilities such as steel mills, foundries, and aluminium smelters. It is typically clean and homogeneous, enabling direct reintroduction into furnaces without entering external recycling markets [ 57 ]. Fabrication or prompt scrap is produced during the manufacturing of metal products. Although it may require minimal processing, fabrication scrap generally retains high material quality and a well-known composition, making it relatively easy to recycle [ 57 ,  58 ].

By contrast, EoL scrap offers high recovery potential but is heterogeneous in both composition and form. Heterogeneity arises because EoL scrap is sourced from diverse products—ranging from vehicles and appliances to construction materials—each containing multiple alloys, coatings, and embedded components. Contaminants further complicate recycling: coatings (paints, galvanization), non-metallic attachments (plastics, glass, rubber), and hazardous residues (oils, lead, or heavy metals) must often be removed before remelting [ 59 ,  60 – 61 ]. A particularly critical issue is the presence of tramp elements—metallic impurities such as copper and tin in steel or iron in aluminium—that accumulate during repeated recycling cycles and cannot be fully removed through conventional refining. Even in small concentrations, tramp elements can degrade mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, or ductility, thereby limiting the suitability of recycled metal for high-quality applications [ 62 ,  63 ]. These challenges not only increase processing costs but also heighten the risk of downcycling, where scrap is converted into lower-grade products. Thus, the type and quality of scrap directly influence recycling efficiency and determine its actual contribution to decarbonization pathways.

sections.heading: Methods
paragraphs: A literature search was conducted to collate relevant papers, books, and reports on the metal scrap value chain and its role in supporting green manufacturing and industrial decarbonization. Because the topic spans multiple domains—including metallurgy, waste management, process engineering, market structure, and policy—the review followed a targeted, problem-driven approach.

Academic literature was identified through iterative keyword searches in major databases, including Scopus, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, and Google Scholar. Search terms were adapted to the analytical needs of each value-chain stage, using combinations such as  scrap collection ,  scrap sorting ,  tramp elements ,  secondary steelmaking ,  electric arc furnace (EAF) ,  scrap quality ,  end-of-life metals , and  metal recycling technologies . When gaps emerged—such as impurity constraints in recycling, sector-specific scrap characteristics, or national policy instruments—supplementary targeted searches were conducted to deepen coverage. Grey literature, including technical reports, statistical yearbooks, and policy documents from credible international organizations and industry associations, was also incorporated to capture operational data, sectoral scrap flows, recycling performance, and regulatory developments that are often underrepresented in academic publications. These materials were selected based on institutional credibility and their relevance to the objectives of the review.

The assembled sources were synthesized using a thematic structure aligned with the predefined stages of the metal scrap value chain: scrap generation, collection, separation and pre-processing, melting and refining, and fabrication and use. This value-chain perspective enables systematic analysis of both technical constraints and institutional factors affecting scrap utilization across different stages of the recycling system. To complement the literature synthesis, an international benchmarking analysis was conducted focusing on five major steel-producing economies: China, the European Union, the United States, Japan, and Türkiye. These cases were selected because they represent diverse steel production structures, scrap supply conditions, and policy frameworks. The benchmarking analysis compares key dimensions of scrap systems across these economies, including scrap availability, steelmaking technology mix, processing infrastructure, regulatory instruments, and circular-economy strategies. The insights derived from this comparison are subsequently synthesized to identify transferable lessons relevant to emerging scrap markets, particularly in the context of Indonesia.

sections.heading: Metal scrap value chain
paragraphs: The concept of a value chain refers to the interconnected activities and processes that add value to a resource as it moves from its point of origin to its final application. In the context of recycling, a value chain captures not only the physical transformation of discarded materials into secondary raw materials but also the economic and environmental value created at each stage. Metal scrap value chain encompasses the processes that transform discarded or residual metal into inputs for new production. The structure of value chain differs depending on the source of scrap. Home and fabrication scrap follows shorter loops. By contrast, EoL is the most complex stream as it requires organized collection, separation, pre-processing, and refining before being reintegrated into production. sections.heading: Collection
paragraphs: Collection is the first and arguably most decisive stage in the scrap value chain, since it determines not only the volume of material recovered but also its quality and level of contamination. While all types of scrap—home, fabrication, and EoL—enter collection pathways in some form, their contributions to market supply differ substantially.

Home scrap is typically recycled internally and rarely enters external markets [ 59 ]. Its clean and homogeneous quality ensures high recovery, but process efficiency improvements have steadily reduced its availability, with home scrap now accounting for only around 10% of total output [ 65 ]. Fabrication scrap plays a more direct role in external scrap markets and is typically collected through scrap dealers or direct contractual arrangements between manufacturers and recyclers [ 66 ]. Its predictable composition and high recovery make it a short-cycle and reliable contributor, although volumes remain constrained by manufacturing scale. As shown in Table  1 , generation coefficients vary widely across sectors, with more intensive forming, stamping, or machining processes generating proportionally higher prompt scrap [ 67 ,  68 – 69 ]. This relationship is confirmed by empirical studies of manufacturing scrap flows, which show that raw-material losses are strongly associated with stamping and machining operations in metal-mechanical production systems [ 70 ]. Alloy composition and contamination risk also vary: automotive and machinery fabrication typically produce clean sheet steel blanks [ 71 ,  72 ], while electronics manufacturing yields thin-gauge steel components often associated with multi-material assemblies [ 73 ,  74 ]. EoL scrap has its supply tied to product lifetimes, meaning that today’s consumption becomes tomorrow’s obsolete scrap after a lag of years or decades. Product lifetimes vary widely across sectors—for example, construction steel used in buildings and infrastructure may remain in service for several decades, whereas vehicles, appliances, and packaging products typically have much shorter service lives, resulting in significantly different timing and volumes of scrap return to the market [ 75 ,  76 ]. Global EoL flows are rising sharply: electronic waste reached 62 Mt in 2022, an 82% increase since 2010, yet only 22.3% was formally collected, representing an estimated US$62 billion in lost recoverable resources [ 64 ]. Construction and demolition waste amounted to 1.68 kg per person per day globally in 2018 [ 77 ], while in the EU packaging waste reached 186.5 kg per inhabitant in 2022, with 4.9% comprising metal packaging [ 78 ]. In the US, consumer electronics, aluminium packaging, and aluminium goods were among the most significant contributors [ 79 ,  80 ].

As summarized in Table  2 , the quality of recovered scrap varies widely due to differences in steel grade, alloying level, and surface treatments across applications. The construction sector predominantly contains low-alloy carbon steels [ 81 ]; automotive and machinery applications incorporate coated steels and higher-alloy grades such as advanced high-strength steel (AHSS) and tool steels [ 82 ,  83 – 84 ], and electronics and appliance scrap tends to consist of thin-gauge steel that is strongly associated with plastics, coatings, and other materials [ 85 ,  86 ]. Steel packaging products have extremely short service lifetimes—typically days to a few months—resulting in rapid generation of end-of-life scrap. Despite this short lifecycle, recovery rates are relatively high due to well-established recycling systems for steel packaging, ranging between 65 and 80% and reaching even higher levels in advanced waste-management systems where bottom ash metal recovery is implemented [ 87 ,  88 – 89 ]. These differences imply that even global EoL scrap flows increase in volume, the timing, accessibility, and metallurgical quality of recovered scrap remain highly heterogeneous. The diversity of actors engaged in EoL scrap collection is illustrated in Fig.  3  [ 90 ]. In emerging economies, informal actors dominate the early stages of collection, performing labour-intensive recovery that feeds into larger dealers and eventually to formal recyclers or exporters. Evidence from multiple cities—including Beijing, Johannesburg, Rio de Janeiro, Rawalpindi, and Colombia—shows that informal networks function as the primary link between waste generators and recycling industries [ 91 ,  92 ,  93 ,  94 – 95 ]. While they play a critical role in diverting metals from landfills and incineration, their operations often lack regulatory oversight, occupational safety measures, and integration with formal systems [ 96 ,  97 ,  98 ,  99 – 100 ]. In advanced economies, by contrast, collection is increasingly dominated by formalized systems. Source-separation systems are widely implemented to enhance recovery rates and improve material purity [ 101 ]. Formalized systems also rely on mandatory take-back programs, which ensure proper treatment of growing e-waste streams and prevent environmental and health risks associated with unsafe disposal [ 102 ]. Source separation of municipal solid waste (MSW) is additionally recognized as a critical driver of high-quality recycling. Empirical studies show that increasing the Source Separation Rate and Separated Transportation Rate significantly improves downstream recycling outcomes and reduces environmental burdens [ 103 ,  104 ]. Regulatory frameworks such as the EU’s Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE) and Restriction of Hazardous Substances (RoHS) directives embed Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) into collection systems, assigning manufacturers responsibility for end-of-life management [ 105 ,  106 ,  107 – 108 ]. These producer-funded models are integrated into broader circular economy strategies that promote eco-design, waste prevention, and material recovery, while also supporting resource security for critical raw materials [ 109 ].

More recently, digital tools such as mobile collection platforms, blockchain-based tracking, and reverse logistics applications are emerging to improve transparency and efficiency in both Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and non-OECD contexts [ 110 ,  111 ,  112 ,  113 ,  114 ,  115 ,  116 – 117 ]. However, in many developing economies—including Indonesia—collection remains dominated by informal actors, with weak implementation of EPR schemes and limited integration into formal recycling networks.

sections.heading: Separation and pre-processing
paragraphs: Scrap must undergo separation and pre-processing to improve material quality, reduce contamination, and prepare feedstock for smelting and refining. This stage act as the “quality gatekeepers,” ensuring that only usable and cost-effective secondary inputs reach downstream furnaces. It is particularly critical for EoL scrap, where heterogeneity and contamination are prevalent. Contaminants such as coatings, plastics, oils, and tramp elements must often be removed or reduced to ensure recyclability and product quality.

Manual sorting represents the most basic form of separation and remains widespread in the informal recycling sector. Workers visually identify and handpick materials, sometimes using simple handheld magnets to distinguish ferrous from non-ferrous metals. In small-scale settings, manual sorting can also include coarse classification of ferrous grades (e.g., light vs. heavy steel). While this process helps divert significant volumes of metal from waste streams, it is inefficient, labour-intensive, and often hazardous due to poor occupational safety standards [ 118 ,  119 ].

In formal recycling operations, a range of automated separation technologies is employed. Magnetic separation is standard in automotive shredding facilities and steel recycling plants, with high-gradient magnetic separation (HGMS) recover weakly magnetic alloys and steel slag residues [ 120 ], while weak magnetic separation (WMS) is effective for steel slag [ 121 ,  122 ]. Due to the strong magnetic properties of ferrous metals, magnetic separation systems can achieve recovery efficiencies often exceeding 90–95% for steel scrap in well-designed recycling facilities [ 123 ]. Eddy current separators are commonly used to recover non-ferrous materials from mixed shredder residues (such as in automotive and appliance recycling stream), with studies have reported 80–95% recovery rates for aluminium and copper [ 124 ,  125 – 126 ]. Density-based methods, such as sink–float or air classification, are widely used in construction and demolition (C&D) waste treatment to separate light and heavy metals at relatively low energy cost [ 127 ]. More advanced systems including sensor-based sorting, such X-ray Fluorescence (XRF), X-ray Diffraction (XRD), and Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy (LIBS), enables high-precision elemental and structural classification, allowing metals and alloys to be classified in real time in high-value recycling streams such as stainless steel, aerospace alloys, and electronic waste [ 128 ]. Each method has strengths and limitations: XRF is fast but limited to surface elements [ 129 ,  130 ]; XRD provides detailed crystallographic information but is slower and less sensitive to elemental composition [ 131 ]; LIBS offers broad elemental detection but faces challenges with detection efficiency and reproducibility [ 132 ,  133 – 134 ]. New hybrid approaches, such as combining LIBS with laser-induced extreme ultraviolet (XUV) spectroscopy (LIXS), have improved sensitivity and reliability [ 135 ]. Furthermore, these techniques are increasingly enhanced with artificial intelligence and machine learning, improving their ability to detect alloys and tramp elements in complex scrap streams [ 136 ,  137 ].

Beyond separation, pre-processing technologies prepare metals for furnace charging by improving logistics, furnace efficiency, and contaminant removal. Shredding and crushing release metals from assemblies, increase surface area for furnace loading, and are standard in automotive and appliance recycling [ 138 ,  139 ]. Contamination control is achieved through washing, chemical cleaning, or thermal de-coating, which remove oils, paints, plastics, or hazardous residues [ 140 ,  141 ]. Baling and briquetting reduce the volume of light scrap (e.g., cans, wires, sheets), facilitating handling and transport, though uneven melting can occur [ 142 ,  143 – 144 ]. Oversized industrial scrap is often reduced through shearing or torch cutting, preparing it for furnace charging [ 145 ,  146 – 147 ].

As summarized in Table  3 , separation and pre-processing methods vary in recovery efficiency, energy and carbon implications, and sectoral adoption. Mature technologies such as magnetic and eddy current separation enable high-volume recovery of common metals, while advanced methods like sensor-based sorting are critical for complex alloys and high-value streams such as e-waste and aerospace scrap. Yet advanced systems remain concentrated in high-income regions, while developing economies rely heavily on manual or basic methods that limit recovery rates. Increasing product complexity—including multi-material vehicles, electronics, and coated construction materials—further challenges existing systems. Emerging innovations such as AI-driven sorting, plasma de-coating, and design-for-disassembly show promise but require broader investment, technological diffusion, and supportive policy frameworks to scale globally. sections.heading: Melting and refining
paragraphs: The melting and refining stage is decisive in determining how much recycled scrap can be incorporated into steel, aluminium, or other metal products without compromising mechanical properties, product performance, or downstream manufacturability. Aluminium is included as a comparison because it represents one of the most mature global recycling systems and demonstrates some of the highest energy savings from secondary production, making it a useful benchmark for evaluating the decarbonization potential of scrap utilization [ 148 ,  149 ]. In primary metal production, molten metal is generated from ore through energy-intensive reduction and smelting processes—such BF–BOF for steel, or the Bayer–Hall–Héroult sequence for aluminium. The secondary route relies on scrap melting, which requires substantially lower thermal input. As summarized in Table  4 , secondary production can reduce energy intensity by 75–80% for steel and over 90% for aluminium compared with primary routes. Table 4 Primary vs. secondary production characteristics for major recycled metals (steel and aluminium) Element Steel Aluminium Primary manufacturing route BF-BOF [ 150 ] Bayer Process & Hall–Héroult [ 151 ] Secondary manufacturing route Scrap EAF [ 152 ] Conventional Remelting [ 153 ] Primary energy intensity (GJ/t)  ~ 18.6 GJ/t [ 154 ] 20.3 GJ/t [ 155 ] 24.1 GJ/t [ 156 ] 144.6 GJ/t [ 157 ] 162 GJ/t [ 158 ] Secondary energy intensity (GJ/t) 5 GJ/t [ 159 ] 10.08 GJ/t [ 158 ] 9.2 GJ/t [ 157 ] Primary CO 2  intensity (t CO 2 /t metal) 1.9 t CO 2 /t [ 154 ] 1.99 t CO 2 /t for BF-BOF [ 160 ] 12 t CO 2 /t Al [ 158 ] 14.77 t CO 2 /t [ 157 ] Secondary CO 2  intensity (t CO 2 /t metal)  ~ 0.27 t CO 2 /t [ 160 ]  ~ 0.6 t CO 2 /t Al [ 158 ] 0.657t CO 2 /t [ 157 ]

Secondary metal production also significantly reduce CO 2  intensity (~ 85–86% for steel and ~ 95% for aluminium). However, the extent to which these benefits can be realized depends strongly on scrap quality, alloy contamination, and impurity profiles. While clean and homogeneous scrap streams can be re-melted with minimal intervention, EoL scrap is inherently heterogeneous and contaminated with coatings, tramp metals, plastics, lubricants, ceramics, and mixed alloys [ 161 ,  162 ]. These impurities are often difficult—or thermodynamically impossible—to remove once melted, making the melting and refining stage the primary technical bottleneck for high-grade recycling. As shown in Table  5 , impurity sources differ substantially by sector: construction scrap commonly contains copper (Cu) and tin (Sn) that contribute to embrittlement and surface cracking; automotive scrap carries Zn from galvanizing and Cu from wiring; and e-waste scrap may contain Pb and other heavy metals that impair weldability and pose environmental hazards [ 163 ,  164 ]. During melting, impurities partition between metal, slag, and off-gas streams depending on oxidation potential, solubility, and vapor pressure. Cu and Sn remain dissolved in molten steel and cannot be selectively oxidized, leading to hot shortness and surface cracking during hot rolling [ 165 ,  166 – 167 ]. Zn volatilizes at steelmaking temperatures, increasing dust loads and stressing gas-cleaning systems [ 168 ,  169 – 170 ]. Pb and other low-melting-point elements volatilize as well, creating environmental and occupational risks [ 171 ,  172 ].

The furnace technology used in steelmaking strongly influences impurity tolerance. BOFs are typically limited to around 20–30% scrap input due to sensitivity to Cu, Sn, and Cr [ 171 ,  173 ], which accumulate in the melt and degrade ductility and corrosion resistance in flat-rolled steel products. EAFs can theoretically operate on 100% scrap, but high-grade flat steel production requires extremely low-residual feedstock [ 174 ]. Producers therefore blend prompt scrap with pre-sorted EoL scrap and, where impurity levels are high, may supplement with virgin ore to dilute tramp elements. High-residual EoL scrap streams are often downcycled into long products, where impurity tolerances are more forgiving [ 163 ,  165 ,  175 ].

In EAF steelmaking, process practices such as hot-heel operation, foamy-slag practice, and oxygen lancing improve thermal efficiency and facilitate impurity partitioning into slag, but they cannot remove tramp elements outright [ 176 ,  177 – 178 ]. Secondary refining technologies—including ladle furnaces (LF), vacuum degassing (VD/VOD), and argon oxygen decarburization (AOD)—help remove dissolved gases and adjust alloy chemistry [ 165 ,  179 ,  180 – 181 ], but cannot eliminate metallic residuals. Consequently, upstream scrap segregation and high-precision sorting are essential to ensure that scrap entering the furnace is compatible with intended downstream products. Emerging processes such as thermal de-zincing, motor pre-shredding, plasma-based decoating, or DRI dilution further complement downstream refining but add cost and generate additional residues [ 182 ]. In aluminium recycling, the impurity profile differs but presents analogous limitations. Tramp elements such as Mg, Fe, Cu, and Si constrain alloy compatibility and limit closed-loop recycling [ 183 ,  184 ]. Automotive aluminium scrap is especially challenging due to alloy mixing, embedded fasteners, and coatings. Refining technologies such chlorine fluxing, argon bubbling, rotary furnace technology, and metal filtration can be used to remove dissolved hydrogen, inclusions, and oxide films, but alloy cross-contamination is often irreversible [ 185 ,  186 ,  187 – 188 ]. Fluxing and salt-based refining technologies can remove some impurities, but they generate environmentally problematic salt-slag wastes that require dedicated recovery or disposal [ 189 ,  190 ]. For packaging scrap, lacquers and coatings must be removed through thermal decoating to minimize dross formation [ 191 ,  192 ].

Tramp element accumulation—especially Cu and Sn in steel; Mg and Si in aluminium; and Pb/ As/Sb in copper—remains the most persistent barrier to high-quality secondary production. Repeated recycling cycles increase residual levels, progressively narrowing the range of products that can meet specification [ 163 ,  193 ,  194 ]. This is why high-quality or specialty products—such as automotive exposed-panel steels and aerospace aluminium alloys—still rely partially on primary metal inputs, even in regions with advanced scrap collection and sorting.

sections.heading: Fabrication and use
paragraphs: Fabrication and use represent the final stages of the metal value chain and play a decisive role in determining not only the volume of scrap generated but also its quality and suitability for high-value secondary production. While much of the literature focuses on collection, sorting, and melting of secondary metal production [ 56 ,  153 ,  195 ,  196 ], the characteristics of future scrap are largely shaped upstream through design and fabrication choices. The selection of materials, manufacturing processes, product architecture, joining decisions, and operational conditions ultimately determines whether scrap returns as clean, high-purity material suitable for closed-loop recycling or as a heterogeneous stream requiring downcycling [ 197 ,  198 ,  199 – 200 ].

During fabrication, industries generate substantial quantities of prompt scrap that is typically clean, homogeneous, and compositionally consistent. Automotive sheet offcuts, appliance panel trimmings, and reinforcement bar offcuts are examples of high-quality prompt scrap that can be directly reintegrated into closed-loop recycling systems [ 201 ,  202 – 203 ]. This predictable chemistry minimizes refining requirements and supports higher-grade secondary products [ 161 ,  204 ,  205 ]. In practice, prompt scrap is rarely mixed with heterogeneous end-of-life (EoL) scrap streams or redirected to primary extraction routes for purification. Primary metallurgical processes such as BF–BOF steelmaking or the Bayer–Hall–Héroult aluminium route are designed for ore-based feedstocks and are not optimized to remove tramp elements introduced through scrap. Moreover, mixing high-purity prompt scrap with contaminated EoL material can degrade feedstock quality and reduce the ability to produce high-grade secondary products. For this reason, industrial recycling systems typically prioritize maintaining the segregation of clean prompt scrap streams and blending them selectively with lower-quality scrap only when necessary to control residual element concentrations.

At the same time, modern products increasingly incorporate complex alloys, fasteners, polymeric components, and embedded electronics, which may hinder disassembly and introduce impurities at EoL [ 163 ,  165 ,  206 ,  207 ]. Design attributes that enhance in-use performance can therefore reduce scrap quality and shift recycling toward lower-value pathways [ 61 ,  208 ,  209 ]. Table  6  summarizes how specific design and fabrication factors influence scrap purity and recyclability outcomes. Material selection strongly influences impurity pathways [ 210 ,  211 ]. High-performance steels and advanced aluminium alloys incorporate alloying additions such as Cr, Ni, Mo, Mn, Cu, and Si, many of which cannot be removed during melting and thus accumulate in recycled feedstock [ 61 ,  163 ,  212 ,  213 ]. Mixed-alloy designs—including aluminium–steel hybrids or cast–wrought aluminium assemblies—are particularly challenging, as alloy incompatibility limits closed-loop recycling without precision separation [ 161 ,  214 ].

Coatings and surface treatments also affect scrap quality. Zn coatings on galvanized steel volatilize during melting, increasing dust generation and zinc loads in off-gas system [ 181 ,  182 ]. Paints, lacquers, enamels, and polymeric coatings introduce organic contaminants that burn off, increasing emissions and slag formation [ 141 ,  153 ,  215 ]. Sn coatings in packaging steel can also introduce metallic impurities that affect inclusion chemistry and melt behaviour [ 216 ,  217 ].

Joining and assembly methods significantly influence dismantling and downstream sorting efficiency [ 218 ,  219 – 220 ]. Welded or laser-joined structures require shredding at EoL, which increases alloy mixing and contaminant dispersion [ 175 ,  218 ,  221 ]. Mechanical fasteners can embed copper or mixed-alloy components into ferrous scrap streams when not removed, increasing Cu contamination in EAF melts [ 166 ].

The integration of embedded electronics and mechatronics further intensifies impurity challenges [ 222 ,  223 – 224 ]. Sensors, wiring harnesses, printed circuit boards, and motors introduce Cu, Sn, Pb, ceramics, and other contaminants that are difficult to remove prior to shredding. In steel recycling, Cu and Sn from wiring and solder are especially problematic because they remain in solution and cause hot shortness during rolling [ 165 ].

Machining and forming processes introduce additional contamination pathways. Machining chips often contain lubricants and fine particulates that require de-oiling or thermal treatment before remelting [ 225 ,  226 ]. During the use phase, corrosion, wear, dirt accumulation, and repairs further degrade scrap quality, widening the gap between clean prompt scrap and heterogeneous EoL scrap [ 161 ,  227 ,  228 ].

These fabrication- and use-phase characteristics determine whether metals circulate in closed-loop or open-loop recycling systems. Clean, well-segregated prompt scrap supports high-quality closed-loop pathways such as automotive sheet-to-sheet recycling or can-to-can aluminium recycling [ 229 ]. In contrast, EoL scrap from complex, multi-material assemblies typically enters open-loop pathways, where residual elements and alloy incompatibilities restrict upgrading and result in downcycling [ 165 ,  208 ,  214 ]. Thus, upstream design and fabrication decisions exert long-term influence on the circularity potential of metals.

High-quality scrap streams generated through thoughtful product design, material standardization, and clean manufacturing practices can substantially reduce refining energy demands, limit tramp element accumulation, and expand the share of secondary production that can substitute for virgin materials. Strengthening design-for-recycling, improving dismantlability, and maintaining scrap segregation across product lifecycles are therefore essential for a low-carbon metal industry.

sections.heading: International benchmarking of metal scrap management
paragraphs: To identify transferable lessons and structural contrasts relevant to industrial decarbonization, this section benchmarks metal scrap systems across five major steel-producing economies: China, the European Union, the United States, Japan, and Türkiye. The benchmarking discusses several dimensions including scrap supply–demand balance and market structure, steelmaking routes, scrap processing and absorption capacity, governance and institutional arrangements, and the role of scrap in steel-sector decarbonization.

sections.heading: China
paragraphs: China is the world’s largest consumer of steel scrap, with total scrap consumption reaching 209.67 Mt in 2024 [ 230 ]. As shown in Fig.  4 , scrap consumption has expanded broadly in line with crude steel production and domestic steel demand over the past decade. This reflects a structurally tight domestic scrap system, in which scrap generation and utilization remain closely matched and leave little room for sustained net imports or stock accumulation. Fig. 4 China steel production, steel consumption, scrap generation, and scrap consumption, 2010–2025.  Source: Authors’ compilation based on data from World Steel Association and Bureau of International Recycling

Despite the scale of scrap use, China’s steel production remains overwhelmingly dominated by BF–BOF, accounting for approximately 80–90% of total output [ 231 ,  232 ]. Around 68% of total scrap is consumed within BF–BOF operations, rather than in EAFs [ 233 ]. Given China’s enormous crude steel output—exceeding 900 million tons in 2023—even modest BOF scrap input ratios translate into very large absolute scrap demand, estimated at approximately 165 Mt [ 234 ]. In contrast, EAF operations account for only about 10% of steel production and face persistent structural disadvantages, including higher electricity costs, inconsistent scrap supply, and weaker purchasing power relative to integrated steelmakers. These factors constrain the expansion of scrap-intensive steelmaking despite government targets to raise the EAF share to 15% by 2025 [ 235 ].

China’s scrap supply is overwhelmingly domestic. In 2024, ferrous scrap imports amounted to only ~ 0.10% (0.2 Mt) of total scrap consumption, while exports remained minimal due to strong internal demand [ 236 ]. The domestic scrap stream is increasingly dominated by EoL scrap (58%), followed by prompt scrap (25%) and home scrap (17%) [ 237 ]. This composition reflects the relatively short average service life of steel products in China—around 25 years, compared with a global average of approximately 40 years—indicating that large volumes of installed steel are now reaching end-of-life. Consequently, domestic scrap availability is expected to continue increasing over the coming decades [ 234 ].

Scrap collection is concentrated in urban and industrial centers and is primarily conducted by small collectors using light vehicles, while urban transport regulations and time-of-day restrictions increase logistical costs and limit efficiency at the collection stage [ 238 ,  239 ]. Despite these constraints, processing capacity has expanded rapidly: by 2021, China operated 584 scrap processing plants with a combined capacity of approximately 150 million tons of obsolete scrap per year, alongside 100–120 Mt of home and prompt scrap generated annually [ 234 ]. Nevertheless, the sector remains highly fragmented. Informal collectors and small, often unlicensed enterprises dominate collection and basic processing, handling an estimated 17–35% of urban recycling activities, resulting in uneven quality control and limited traceability [ 240 ] Although consolidation is underway—particularly through integration by major steel enterprises—regional concentration remains high, with more than 80% of scrap supply concentrated in 12 provinces and municipalities [ 234 ].

China’s scrap governance framework is strongly state-led. Historically regulated under the broader solid waste regime, scrap imports were sharply restricted through revisions to the Catalogue of Solid Waste Used as Raw Materials in 2018–2019, which imposed licensing, inspection, and enforcement requirements. While these measures initially constrained access to high-quality imported scrap, they also accelerated investment in domestic collection and pre-processing capacity. In 2021, new technical standards reclassified certain high-grade ferrous and stainless steel scrap as “recycled raw materials,” improving quality control without materially increasing import volumes [ 234 ,  241 ]. Scrap plays an increasingly important but still constrained role in China’s steel sector. Higher scrap use offers substantial potential to reduce energy intensity and emissions, yet the continued dominance of BF–BOF production limits the extent to which scrap can displace primary iron inputs. Structural barriers—including electricity pricing, grid emissions, and market power asymmetries between BF–BOF and EAF producers—continue to slow the expansion of scrap-intensive steelmaking [ 235 ].

sections.heading: European union
paragraphs: The EU is a leading player in the global steel scrap value chain, both as a major consumer of scrap and as one of the world’s top scrap exporters. In 2024, EU scrap consumption reached 76.65 Mt [ 242 ]. However, this short-term recovery masks a longer-term structural contraction of the EU steel sector. As shown in Fig.  5 , crude steel production declined substantially from > 200 Mt in the mid-2000s to ~ 129 Mt in 2024, accompanied by a parallel decline in steel consumption and scrap use. Despite this contraction, the EU consistently generates more scrap than it consumes, resulting in a structural surplus at the regional level. Fig. 5 EU steel production, steel consumption, scrap production, and scrap consumption, 2006–2025.  Source: Authors’ compilation based on data from World Steel Association and Eurofer

In 2024, domestic scrap generation reached approximately 88 Mt, exceeding consumption and enabling net exports of 16.29 Mt [ 242 ]. Scrap imports remain modest, averaging around 4.9% of total consumption between 2006 and 2024, and are driven primarily by quality considerations rather than supply shortages [ 243 ]. The EU scrap stream is dominated by post-consumer material (~ 79% in 2024), while pre-consumer “prime” scrap constitutes only a small share [ 244 ]. This imbalance between quantity and quality plays a central role in shaping EU scrap trade patterns. Lower-quality post-consumer scrap is disproportionately exported—primarily to countries such as Türkiye, India, and Egypt—while higher-quality scrap is largely retained within the EU to meet domestic steelmaking requirements.

The structure of the EU steel industry reinforces the importance of scrap quality. Electric arc furnace (EAF) steelmaking accounted for approximately 44.6% of EU steel production in 2024 (~ 57.8 Mt) [ 242 ]. Although this share has increased over time, the pace of transition has been relatively slow. One of the key constraints is the limited availability of low-residual, high-quality scrap, which is critical given the dominance of automotive manufacturing and mechanical engineering in EU steel demand. When lower-grade post-consumer scrap is used, producers often dilute impurities with virgin iron units, increasing costs and reducing the economic advantage of scrap-based production [ 244 ].

The EU’s high scrap recovery rates are supported by a highly formalized and technologically advanced waste management system. End-of-life steel-containing products are collected and processed through licensed facilities operating under stringent environmental and safety standards. The End-of-Life Vehicles (ELV) Directive mandates 95% recovery and at least 85% recycling by weight, ensuring a steady flow of ferrous scrap from the automotive sector [ 245 ]. Large, specialized processors employ advanced shredding and sorting technologies, enabling standardized scrap grades suitable for steelmaking. As a result, approximately 90% of steel products reaching end-of-life in the EU are recoverable [ 246 ].

Governance of scrap flows in the EU is closely integrated with circular economy and climate policy frameworks. Transboundary movement of scrap is regulated under the EU Waste Shipment Regulation (WSR), which governs exports unless scrap attains end-of-waste status. Concerns over large exports to regions with lower environmental standards have intensified policy scrutiny, particularly after ferrous scrap exports peaked at approximately 19 Mt in 2021, with Türkiye accounting for around 60% of extra-EU exports [ 242 ,  244 ]. To improve transparency, the European Commission introduced a customs surveillance mechanism in 2025 under the EU Steel and Metals Action Plan, enabling monthly monitoring of scrap trade flows [ 247 ].

Scrap occupies a central role in the EU’s steel transition strategy. The EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) creates a strong economic incentive for scrap-based steelmaking by internalizing the carbon cost of primary production routes. Compared to BF–BOF steelmaking, EAF production using scrap exhibits substantially lower emissions intensity, reinforcing demand for high-quality scrap feedstock [ 248 ].

sections.heading: United States
paragraphs: The US serves as a major consumer, exporter, and importer of scrap. As shown in Fig.  6 , scrap consumption closely follows crude steel production over time. In 2024, the US consumed ~ 63 Mt of steel scrap, exported ~ 16 Mt, and imported ~ 4.7 Mt [ 249 ]. As the fourth-largest crude steel producer globally, with output of approximately 81 Mt in 2024, the steel sector is structurally oriented toward scrap-based production, with EAFs accounting for about 72% of total steel output [ 249 ]. Fig. 6 US steel production, steel consumption, scrap production and consumption, 2000–2025.  Source: Authors’ compilation based on data from USGS

The US scrap supply–demand balance is broadly near-balanced at the national level, supported by substantial domestic scrap generation. In 2024, total scrap generation reached approximately 73.6 Mt, exceeding scrap consumption and enabling significant exports while still supporting domestic EAF operations [ 250 ]. As indicated in Fig.  6 , periods of cyclical downturn—such as the 2008–2009 financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic—were accompanied by synchronized declines in steel production, consumption, and scrap use. Scrap trade patterns are shaped by quality differentiation rather than volume scarcity. Lower-grade scrap is typically exported to countries such as Türkiye, Mexico, and India, while higher-quality scrap—primarily from Canada—is imported to support applications requiring tighter impurity control [ 251 ,  252 ].

The dominance of EAF technology has important implications for scrap processing requirements. Scrap used as EAF feedstock must meet relatively high purity standards, necessitating effective sorting and preparation. US scrap processing relies on magnetic separation, visual identification, and advanced sorting technologies, supported by standardized grading and pre-processing systems operated by large, vertically integrated steel producers and recycling firms [ 253 ,  254 ]. Although the scrap ecosystem is heterogeneous, informal collection (“scrapping”) plays a secondary role, persisting alongside formal operations but remaining limited in scale and difficult to quantify [ 255 ].

The regulatory framework governing scrap management in the United States is primarily defined by the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) and its implementing regulations. Under RCRA, certain categories of processed home and prompt scrap are excluded from classification as solid waste, while other recyclable scrap metals are exempt from hazardous-waste regulation provided they are legitimately recycled (40 CFR 261.6). By distinguishing recyclable scrap from hazardous waste, this framework lowers compliance barriers while preserving oversight for environmentally risky materials, providing regulatory certainty that supports high recycling rates and market liquidity.

Scrap plays a central role in the US steel sector. The high penetration of EAF technology enables relatively low emissions intensity compared with BF–BOF-based systems, positioning scrap-based steelmaking as a key contributor to emissions reduction [ 256 ]. However, regional variation in electricity carbon intensity and the limited tolerance of EAFs for lower-grade scrap constrain further expansion of scrap use without additional processing or dilution. Despite these challenges, recycling performance remains high, with steel recycling rates consistently estimated at 80–90% over the past decade. Automobiles and construction steel remain major scrap sources, with approximately 15 Mt of steel recovered annually from ELV and recycling rates for construction steel approaching 98% [ 250 ].

sections.heading: Japan
paragraphs: Japan is one of the world’s leading ferrous scrap exporters, shipping 6.9 Mt of scrap in 2023, while also being the world’s third-largest crude steel producer, with output of 86.8 Mt in the same year [ 257 ]. A substantial share of these exports is directed to nearby markets, particularly South Korea (38%) and Taiwan (24.3%) [ 258 ]. This export orientation reflects high scrap generation relative to domestic scrap consumption. In 2023, Japan generated approximately 37.6 Mt of scrap while consuming only 31.8 Mt, resulting in a persistent structural surplus that sustains its role as a key supplier within the Asia–Pacific scrap market [ 259 ]. As shown in Fig.  7 , scrap production has consistently exceeded scrap consumption over time, despite fluctuations in crude steel output and domestic demand. Fig.7 Japan steel production, steel consumption, scrap production and consumption, 2011–2025.  Source: Authors’ compilation based on data from World Steel Association and The Japan Ferrous Raw Materials Association

Relatively low domestic scrap demand in Japan is primarily driven by the country’s steelmaking structure. Japanese steel production remains heavily dependent on BF–BOF, which consumes significantly less scrap than EAFs. As a result, the ability of the domestic steel industry to absorb available scrap is inherently limited. Large sunk investments in integrated steelmaking facilities create strong lock-in effects, limiting rapid transition to EAFs [ 260 ]. Moreover, BF–BOF production is better suited to meeting the stringent quality requirements of Japan’s advanced manufacturing sectors, particularly automotive and precision industries [ 261 ]. Energy and climate policy considerations further constrain EAF expansion. Electricity generation in Japan remains carbon intensive, with renewables accounting for only 37.73% of the power mix [ 262 ]. Under climate policy mechanisms such as the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), electricity-related emissions can translate into higher indirect costs for EAF producers, weakening the relative attractiveness of scrap-based steelmaking [ 263 ]. Uncertainty surrounding future electricity prices and power-sector decarbonization further dampens incentives for large-scale EAF investment [ 264 ].

Japan’s scrap system is distinguished by highly formalized waste governance and advanced recycling infrastructure [ 265 ]. In 2023, approximately 47.70% of ferrous scrap originated from obsolete scrap, 32.95% from home scrap, and 19.35% from prompt scrap, reflecting a mature industrial cycle and high collection efficiency [ 259 ,  266 ]. Although annual scrap recovery represents only a small share of cumulative steel stock, sustained institutional commitment has created a robust foundation for long-term circularity [ 267 ]. Japan’s waste governance model [ 268 ,  269 ,  269 ,  270 ]—characterized by clear regulatory responsibility, strong municipal systems, and integration of recycling actors—supports consistently high scrap quality.

At the operational level, ferrous scrap recycling is supported by advanced dismantling and processing technologies. ELVs and appliances are collected under regulated schemes such as the ELV Recycling Law, which mandates component removal prior to shredding [ 271 ] Large-scale shredders and multi-stage separation systems—including magnetic, eddy-current, and sink–float processes—are combined with LIBS and XRF-based composition analysis to control impurities [ 272 ]. Post-shredding treatments and manual removal of copper-bearing components are particularly important, as approximately two-thirds of residual copper accumulation in Japanese scrap originates from insufficient dismantling rather than alloy additions [ 163 ].

These quality-control measures allow Japanese integrated mills to achieve relatively high scrap charging rates in BF–BOF operations under controlled conditions [ 271 ]. Nevertheless, because roughly 75% of Japan’s steel is produced via BF–BOF rather than EAF, national scrap consumption remains lower than in EAF-dominated regions such as the EU and the US [ 273 ]. Despite this structural constraint, Japan’s emphasis on upstream quality control yields recycled steel of exceptionally high purity, with measured copper concentrations in scrap-based rebars (~ 0.32%) comparable to levels observed in Western Europe (~ 0.29%) [ 163 ].

sections.heading: Türkiye
paragraphs: Türkiye’s steel sector is characterized by a strong reliance on EAF technology, which shapes the country’s scrap metal dynamics. The country consumes ~ 31.27 Mt of scrap in 2024 [ 257 ], more than three times its domestic scrap generation (9.87 Mt). 1  As illustrated in Fig.  8 , scrap consumption has consistently exceeded domestic scrap generation over time, underscoring Türkiye’s structural dependence on external scrap supplies. Fig. 8 Republic of Türkiye Steel Production, Steel Consumption, Scrap Production and, 2005–2024.  Source: Authors’ compilation based on data from World Steel Association and Bureau of International Recycling

This imbalance has positioned Türkiye as one of the world’s largest ferrous scrap importers. Most imported scrap originates from the United States, the Netherlands, Lithuania, Belgium, and the UK [ 274 ], making imported scrap an essential an essential input for Turkish steel production. The dominance of EAF-based steelmaking reflects both economic and strategic considerations: EAFs require lower upfront investment than integrated BF–BOF facilities and align with Türkiye’s decarbonization ambitions, particularly given limited domestic iron ore resources [ 275 ]. However, this technological configuration exposes the steel sector to international scrap market volatility and external supply risks.

Low domestic scrap generation is driven by structural and institutional factors. Rapid industrial expansion since the early 2000s has increased steel demand, but many steel-containing products and buildings have not yet reached end-of-life, constraining obsolete scrap availability [ 276 ,  277 – 278 ]. In addition, scrap collection and recycling systems remain underdeveloped and are dominated by informal actors, estimated to account for up to 80% of recycling activities nationwide [ 279 ]. Although municipalities are formally responsible for waste management, weak integration with informal collectors contributes to low recovery rates, with around 61% of waste still disposed of in landfills [ 280 ,  281 ]. Efforts to formalize the sector have faced persistent challenges, including limited fiscal support, weak enforcement, and resistance from stakeholders benefiting from the existing system [ 282 ,  283 ].

Türkiye applies a regulatory approach to metal scrap that differs from those of the EU, US, and Japan. Rather than embedding quality standards within comprehensive recycling legislation, Türkiye relies on import restrictions combined with international scrap specifications. Scrap regulation is governed primarily by Environmental Law No. 2872 and the Waste Management Regulation and By-law on Waste Management (2015). A major policy shift in 2020–2021 introduced requirements for importers to source at least 50% of raw material needs domestically, reflecting concerns over resource security and supply-chain resilience. Despite recent progress, Türkiye’s regulatory framework remains less developed than those of other benchmarked economies.

At the processing stage, most imported scrap consists of Heavy Melting Steel (HMS) grades. Scrap is collected and sorted prior to delivery, then subjected to magnetic separation, shredding, and eddy-current processing to reduce contamination before melting [ 284 ]. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of these downstream processes is constrained by weak upstream separation and inconsistent scrap quality at the collection stage.

sections.heading: Indonesia in comparison
paragraphs: Indonesia shows a different scrap system structure compared with the benchmark economies discussed above. Detailed statistics exist for scrap generation and consumption in China, the EU, the United States, Japan, and Türkiye, whereas publicly available data on Indonesia’s domestic scrap generation and consumption remain limited. Therefore, the dynamics of the Indonesian scrap system are illustrated using indicators of steel production, steel consumption, and scrap trade (imports and exports), as shown in Fig.  9 . Fig.9 Indonesia steel production, steel consumption, scrap import and export, 2011–2023.  Source: Authors’ compilation based on data from World Steel Association

Indonesia’s steel sector has expanded rapidly over the past decade. Steel production increased from approximately 3.7 Mt in 2010 to around 15.6 Mt in 2022, representing an increase of nearly 12 Mt and a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of about 12.8%. Domestic steel consumption also grew steadily during the same period, rising from roughly 10.9 Mt in 2010 to about 18.0 Mt in 2022 (CAGR ≈ 4.3%), although a temporary decline occurred around 2021 following pandemic-related disruptions. Despite the rapid expansion of production capacity, domestic output has not yet fully matched demand, resulting in a persistent gap between national steel consumption and domestic supply.

From a technological perspective, Indonesia’s steelmaking capacity remains dominated by the BF–BOF production route, accounting for approximately 59.3% of total installed capacity, while the remaining share is produced through EAF facilities. This production structure differs from EAF-dominated systems such as the United States and Türkiye and limits the extent to which scrap can serve as the primary feedstock in domestic steelmaking. Scrap trade patterns further reflect structural characteristics of the Indonesian scrap system. Scrap imports fluctuate between roughly 1–2.5 Mt annually, indicating partial reliance on imported secondary feedstock to support domestic steel production. Between 2013 and 2022, imports declined from approximately 2.4 Mt to around 1.2 Mt, while scrap exports remain relatively small and are directed primarily to neighboring Southeast Asian markets.

Indonesia’s scrap ecosystem remains less mature than those of the benchmark economies. In contrast to systems such as the EU and the United States where domestic scrap generation broadly matches or exceeds steel-sector demand, Indonesia’s scrap system is characterized by limited domestic scrap availability and reliance on imported feedstock. The institutional and structural factors underlying these patterns are examined in the following section.

The country-level analyses above highlight substantial variation in scrap supply structures, steelmaking routes, processing sophistication, governance arrangements, and decarbonization relevance across the benchmarked economies.
