sections.heading: Synthesis: lessons and pathways for Indonesia
Key insights from global benchmarking
paragraphs: A key insight from the benchmarking of China, the EU, the US, Japan, and Türkiye is that scrap availability alone does not determine scrap utilization. China and Japan both generate substantial volumes of ferrous scrap, yet domestic absorption remains constrained by the continued dominance of BF–BOF [ 231 ,  232 ,  260 ]. In contrast, the US and Türkiye demonstrate that high EAF penetration enables extensive scrap use even under conditions of limited domestic scrap supply, though with differing implications for trade dependence and supply security [ 273 ,  275 ]. These show the importance of aligning scrap strategies with prevailing steelmaking technologies rather than assuming that increased scrap generation will automatically translate into higher utilization.

Beyond furnace configuration, formalized collection systems and high EoL capture rates emerge as foundational enablers of effective scrap markets. The EU, the US, and Japan rely predominantly on formal waste collection and recycling systems supported by clearly defined institutional responsibilities. In several cases, these systems are reinforced by EPR schemes that stabilize scrap supply and encourage investment in recovery infrastructure [ 245 ,  265 ]. Predictable scrap flows reduce uncertainty for downstream processors and steelmakers, enabling long-term planning and technological upgrading [ 285 ]. In contrast, systems characterized by substantial informal-sector dominance—such as Türkiye and parts of China—face persistent inefficiencies in scrap recovery despite strong downstream demand, leading to supply volatility and quality inconsistencies [ 280 ,  286 ].

The benchmarking further reveals that scrap quality management is as critical as scrap quantity. Advanced economies have invested heavily in sorting, separation, and impurity control technologies, enabling higher scrap charging rates and broader furnace compatibility. Japan represents the most advanced case, where regulated dismantling practices, granular grading standards, and widespread deployment of sensor-based technologies enable high-quality scrap use even in BF–BOF operations [ 271 ,  272 ]. The EU and the US similarly benefit from harmonized standards or market-driven grading systems that facilitate efficient matching between scrap quality and steelmaking requirements [ 163 ].

Another recurring pattern concerns policy coherence across waste, industrial, and climate domains. In the EU and Japan, scrap management is embedded within broader circular economy and sustainability frameworks that explicitly link recycling, industrial competitiveness, and emissions reduction [ 245 ,  265 ]. This coherence provides consistent signals for investment and innovation. By contrast, Türkiye’s reliance on supply-side import restrictions illustrates the limitations of narrowly focused regulatory approaches when not accompanied by upstream improvements in domestic collection, processing, and quality control [ 283 ]. Governance arrangements therefore play a decisive role in shaping long-term scrap system performance.

The benchmarking underscores that scrap’s role in decarbonization is highly context-dependent. In EAF-dominated systems such as the US and Türkiye, scrap is central to emissions reduction, although outcomes depend strongly on electricity carbon intensity and supply security [ 273 ,  275 ]. In BF–BOF-dominated systems such as China and Japan, scrap plays a more incremental role. These differences indicate that effective scrap strategies must be tailored to national industrial and energy contexts rather than applied uniformly.

sections.heading: Indonesia’s scrap industry: structural conditions, gaps, and constraints
paragraphs: When assessed against the global benchmarks, Indonesia’s scrap industry exhibits several structural characteristics that limit its current contribution to green manufacturing and industrial decarbonization. One defining feature is the fragmented nature of scrap collection and recovery, which remains heavily dependent on informal actors, particularly at the household and small-commercial levels. While informal collectors play an important role in recovering recyclable materials, the absence of systematic coordination, standardized sorting, and material traceability results in low recovery rates for high-quality ferrous scrap and significant material losses [ 280 ]. In contrast to the EU, the US, and Japan, Indonesia lacks a national framework that systematically integrates informal collectors into regulated scrap supply chains.

Another critical constraint relates to low end-of-life capture rates for steel-containing products. Indonesia’s rapid infrastructure expansion and industrial growth since the early 2000s have substantially increased steel demand, yet much of the in-use steel stock has not reached the end of its service life [ 276 ,  277 – 278 ]. Even where EoL products are available, weak dismantling practices and limited separation at source constrain scrap quality and usability. This stands in sharp contrast to regulated dismantling systems such as Japan’s ELV framework, which ensures systematic recovery of high-quality scrap [ 271 ].

Limitations in scrap processing and sorting capabilities further constrain Indonesia’s scrap system. Most domestic processing relies on basic mechanical separation, with limited deployment of advanced sensor-based technologies. As a result, impurity levels—particularly copper contamination—remain relatively high, restricting the range of steel products that can be produced using recycled inputs [ 163 ]. Similar challenges are observed in Türkiye, whereas the EU, US, and Japan have largely addressed these issues through sustained investment in processing sophistication. Weak industrial integration between scrap suppliers and steel producers represents an additional barrier. Indonesian steelmakers often treat scrap as a supplementary or opportunistic input rather than as a strategic resource embedded within long-term production planning. This contrasts with EAF-dominated systems in the US and parts of the EU, where steel producers actively shape scrap specifications and quality requirements through market coordination. Limited integration reduces incentives for upstream quality improvement and constrains investment in advanced processing infrastructure.

Governance gaps persist across policy domains. Scrap management in Indonesia is regulated primarily through waste policy, with limited alignment to industrial development strategies or climate mitigation objectives. EPR schemes for steel-intensive products remain underdeveloped, and there is no unified national scrap grading standard comparable to those used in the EU or Japan. These institutional gaps reduce policy coherence and limit the strategic role of scrap in decarbonization planning.

Indonesia’s growing reliance on imported scrap highlights systemic weaknesses in domestic supply. While imports can alleviate short-term shortages, excessive dependence exposes the steel sector to price volatility, trade disruptions, and geopolitical risks, as demonstrated by Türkiye’s experience. Without parallel improvements in domestic scrap recovery and quality, import reliance may undermine long-term industrial resilience.

sections.heading: Priority development pathways for Indonesia’s scrap industry
paragraphs: The benchmarking insights point toward the need for a coordinated, system-level approach to strengthening Indonesia’s scrap industry. One priority pathway involves formalizing and upgrading scrap collection systems through hybrid models that integrate informal collectors into regulated frameworks. Rather than displacing informal actors, such models—drawing on experiences from Japan and parts of the EU—can improve material traceability, increase recovery rates, and support social inclusion through licensing, training, and contractual arrangements [ 287 ,  288 – 289 ].

A second pathway concerns improving end-of-life product management through targeted EPR schemes. Introducing EPR for steel-intensive products such as vehicles, appliances, and construction materials can stabilize scrap supply and incentivize design-for-recycling. The EU’s product-specific directives and Japan’s ELV framework offer transferable lessons for structuring such schemes in Indonesia. At the processing stage, scaling up investment in scrap sorting and separation technologies represents another critical pathway. Public–private partnerships can help overcome the high upfront costs associated with advanced separation technologies. Enhancing scrap quality will expand furnace compatibility, reduce impurity-related yield losses, and improve the economic viability of scrap-based steelmaking [ 290 ,  291 ].

Closer integration between scrap markets and steelmaking routes is also essential. Indonesia’s long-term steel strategy would benefit from explicitly considering the role of EAF expansion, scrap charging optimization in existing furnaces, and alignment with electricity-sector decarbonization pathways. Experiences from the US and the EU demonstrate that coordinated development of furnace technology and scrap quality standards is essential for maximizing emissions reductions.

At the governance level, strengthening policy coherence across waste, industrial, and climate domains constitutes a further priority pathway. Recognizing scrap not merely as waste but as a strategic industrial resource can create consistent policy signals for investment and innovation. Integrated frameworks such as the EU’s circular economy strategy offer useful reference points. At the same time, import reliance should be managed strategically. While imported scrap can play a transitional role, long-term decarbonization and industrial resilience require building domestic scrap capacity. Türkiye’s experience illustrates both the benefits and risks of import-dependent EAF systems, underscoring the importance of balancing trade openness with domestic capacity building [ 275 ]. Taken together, these pathways suggest that Indonesia’s scrap strategy should move beyond incremental improvements toward a coordinated transformation of governance, technology, and industrial integration.

sections.heading: Conclusion and implications
paragraphs: This review examines the metal scrap value chain as a critical enabler of green manufacturing and industrial decarbonization, with a focus on identifying global lessons applicable to Indonesia. By integrating conceptual insights on green manufacturing with a structured value-chain analysis and international benchmarking of five major steel-producing economies—China, the European Union, the United States, Japan, and Türkiye—this study demonstrates that effective scrap utilization depends on coordinated development across technological, institutional, and market dimensions rather than on scrap availability alone.

A key contribution of this review lies in clarifying how decarbonization outcomes are shaped by interactions across distinct stages of the metal scrap value chain. Collection systems determine the volume, spatial distribution, and initial contamination of scrap; separation and pre-processing govern material purity and the feasibility of high-grade recycling; melting and refining impose thermodynamic and metallurgical limits on impurity tolerance and recycled content; and fabrication and product-use decisions influence future scrap quality through alloy choice, coatings, joining methods, and dismantlability. The analysis shows that deficiencies at any single stage—such as weak end-of-life capture or inadequate sorting—can constrain downstream energy and emissions benefits that cannot be fully recovered through metallurgical processing alone. Decarbonization benefits from scrap therefore emerge only when the entire value chain is aligned.

The international benchmarking yields several further insights. First, scrap plays fundamentally different roles across steel systems depending on dominant production routes. In EAF-dominated systems such as the US and Türkiye, scrap serves as the primary feedstock and a central lever for emissions reduction, although outcomes depend on electricity carbon intensity and supply security. In contrast, in BF–BOF-dominated systems such as China and Japan, scrap contributes more incrementally to decarbonization, constrained by technological lock-in and stringent product-quality requirements. Second, formalized collection systems and high end-of-life capture rates are foundational to resilient scrap markets. Countries with clearly defined institutional responsibilities, EPR schemes, and integrated waste governance achieve higher recovery rates and more stable scrap supply. Third, scrap quality management emerges as a decisive factor: investment in advanced sorting, separation, and impurity-control technologies enables higher scrap charging rates, expands furnace compatibility, and increases the economic value of recycled metal. Finally, policy coherence across waste, industrial, and climate domains strongly shapes long-term system performance by influencing investment incentives and technology adoption.

When assessed against these benchmarks, Indonesia’s scrap industry remains constrained by structural gaps across multiple value-chain stages. Informal dominance in collection, low end-of-life capture rates, limited processing sophistication, weak integration between scrap markets and steel producers, and fragmented governance frameworks collectively limit the contribution of scrap to green manufacturing and industrial decarbonization. While scrap imports can partially offset domestic supply shortages, excessive reliance on external markets exposes the steel sector to price volatility and supply risks, potentially undermining long-term industrial resilience.

This study also has several limitations that should be acknowledged. First, the analysis relies primarily on secondary data sources, industry reports, and published studies, which may vary in methodology, reporting scope, and temporal coverage across countries. As a result, direct cross-country comparisons should be interpreted with caution. Second, sectoral estimates of scrap generation, recovery rates, and lifecycle assumptions are derived from available literature and representative datasets rather than harmonized global databases, reflecting the broader lack of standardized reporting in scrap markets. Third, the study adopts a qualitative benchmarking approach to compare national scrap systems; while this provides valuable structural insights, it does not quantify the potential emissions reductions associated with different policy or technological pathways. Future research could address these limitations by developing harmonized datasets on scrap flows, conducting country-level material flow analyses, and integrating techno-economic or life-cycle modelling to estimate the decarbonization potential of improved scrap utilization strategies.

The synthesis presented in this review points to several strategic implications for Indonesia. Strengthening scrap utilization requires a shift from fragmented, incremental interventions toward a coordinated, system-level approach that addresses bottlenecks across the full value chain. Priority actions include formalizing and upgrading scrap collection through inclusive governance models that integrate informal actors; introducing targeted EPR schemes for steel-intensive products to stabilize end-of-life supply; scaling investment in advanced sorting and impurity-management technologies to improve scrap quality; and aligning scrap-market development with steelmaking-route modernization and electricity-sector decarbonization. For industrial practitioners, these findings highlight the importance of maintaining scrap segregation, investing in advanced sorting and pre-processing technologies, and integrating recycling considerations into product design and fabrication practices. For researchers, the study underscores the need for improved datasets on scrap flows, more rigorous cross-country material flow analyses, and integrated techno-economic and life-cycle modelling to better quantify the decarbonization potential of scrap-based production systems. Beyond Indonesia, this review contributes to the broader literature on circular economy and industrial decarbonization by demonstrating the analytical value of benchmarking scrap systems through a structured value-chain perspective. By linking quantitative indicators to stage-specific constraints and system-level characteristics, the study provides a framework for comparing scrap markets across diverse industrial contexts.
